subject: unicornFoal
pitch: A newborn unicorn foal on wobbly long legs. A pearly white coat with a soft lilac shimmer, a short fluffy mane and tail in pastel pink, mint and lavender, a small spiralled horn in gold, big dark eyes with long lashes, little silver hooves, and a daisy chain hanging around its neck.
reasoning:
I'm sketching proportions for a stylized low-poly newborn unicorn foal, planning body length, leg height, head size, and horn scale, with +Y up and the model facing +Z.

For the body I'm using a stretched capsule lying along Z, with chest and rump endpoints defined, and I'm working out leg segments — thigh, knee, cannon bone, fetlock, pastern, and hoof — sized so the body underside and withers land at a believable foal height. I'm also setting up the neck as an angled cylinder connecting the shoulders to an oversized, cute stylized head with a boxy skull and muzzle.

Now I'm detailing the head group itself: positioning the skull, extending the muzzle forward and downward, adding dark nostril spheres, pointy ears with pink interiors, large expressive eyes with highlights and lash details, and a spiraled golden horn built from stacked cones on the forehead.

For the mane I'm clustering small icosahedron spheres along the neck crest in cycling pastel colors, with tufts forming a forelock between the ears. The tail will be several hanging strands of scaled icosahedron chains in pink, mint, and lavender, each about 0.4m long with a slight curve. Around the neck I'm adding a drooping daisy chain made of white-and-yellow flowers linked by green stems, arranged along a catenary loop that hangs lower at the front of the chest.

Each daisy is built from eight small petal shapes around a yellow center disc, connected by tiny green capsule stems, with roughly 14 daisies total keeping the mesh count manageable—around 500 meshes, well within the 1000 limit, so I'll keep using individual meshes rather than instancing.

For the coat material, I'm thinking a pearly white with lilac shimmer using MeshStandardMaterial, low metalness, moderate roughness, possibly layered with a canvas-drawn texture of soft lilac, pink, and mint iridescent blotches to give it that opalescent quality rather than a flat color.

I'm thinking about adding a small cute detail—a tiny gold star cutie mark on each hip, made as a thin extruded star shape embedded slightly into the curved body surface, for a bit of extra charm.

For the foal's features, I want some lavender fuzz tufts at the fetlocks for feathering, and I'm planning a wobbly, splayed-leg stance typical of a nursing foal—front legs slightly offset forward/back and angled outward, hind legs similarly staggered, while making sure all hooves still touch the ground plane. I'll build each leg as a joint chain from hip to knee to fetlock to get that gangly, newborn look.

I'm writing a limb-builder helper that constructs tapered cylinder segments between 3D joint points, orienting each cylinder along the direction vector between the points so I can assemble legs piece by piece from shoulder/hip down through knee and fetlock to hoof.

For the foal's front legs, I'm sketching the forearm-to-knee, cannon, pastern, and hoof segments, keeping proportions exaggeratedly long and leggy. I'm also setting the torso dimensions using a capsule shape rotated to run along the Z axis, narrowed slightly and positioned at body height 0.78.

With withers around 0.95 and overall height to the head roughly 1.25, that's consistent with a realistic newborn foal scale. Now I'm working out the leg attachment points: front legs near x=±0.1, z=0.22, y=0.7, hind legs slightly further back and wider, then building out the front leg geometry from shoulder down through the forearm and knee with tapering joint radii.

Continuing the leg segments down through cannon, fetlock, pastern, and hoof, giving each section its own tapering radius so the hoof flares slightly at the base. I'm also planning a subtle asymmetric wobble pose by offsetting each leg's foot position forward/back and in/out slightly for a natural stance.

For the hind legs I'm sketching a different joint structure with the thigh, stifle bend, gaskin, and hock, mapping out approximate joint coordinates so the hind leg bends believably compared to the straighter front leg.

Let me adjust the hock height to about 0.34, closer to real horse proportions. I'm planning a function to build each leg from a base pose plus offsets scaled by how close a joint is to the ground, so the foot gets the full variation while the hip stays fixed, keeping hooves flat on the ground.

For the hoof itself, I'll keep it a simple vertical tapered cylinder with a flat bottom rather than tilting it along the pastern angle, and offset the pastern slightly forward so the coronet sits just ahead of the fetlock.

For materials, since metal without an environment map renders too dark in three.js, I'll use moderate metalness (around 0.35-0.4) with silver color for hooves and a warm gold with slight emissive glow for the horn so both stay visible under plain lighting. Now moving on to the joint spheres at the knee and fetlock, colored to match the coat.

Below the fetlock I want small lavender/pink tufts, using scaled icosahedrons pointing downward for a cute fuzzy effect, and I'm considering a subtle lilac tint for the lower legs and inner ears to complement the pearly white coat with its lilac shimmer speckling.

For the neck, I'm working out a short, thin, mostly upright cylinder joining chest to head, tapering from a wider base to narrower top, angled around 50 degrees forward with a sphere blending the base into the chest. Then for the head, I'm positioning it at the top of the neck and calculating the pitch rotation needed to tilt it slightly downward.

For the head shape itself, I'm building a rounded skull sphere scaled narrower horizontally, with a tapered muzzle extending forward and down using a flattened cylinder, plus a small chin sphere and a pinkish nose tip at the muzzle's end.

Giving it character details: tiny dark flattened spheres for nostrils placed at the muzzle tip sides, and a thin dark curved shape at the muzzle underside to suggest a soft smiling mouth.

For the cheeks, I'm placing rounded spheres lower on the face for a chubby foal look, with small flattened pink discs near the eyes to add a blush effect. The eyes themselves will sit on the sides of the head as large dark spheres to give that big-eyed foal charm.

Layering out the eye design now: a dark plum sclera, a deep purple iris with gradient, a black pupil, and two white highlight dots, all angled slightly forward using rotation offsets so the eyes appear to face outward naturally.

Now I'm adding eyelashes as thin tapered cylinders fanned along the upper edge of the eyeball, arcing upward and outward in dark plum, positioned using angle-based placement around the eye's local axes.

I'm working through the local axis orientation for each side's eye group — since rotation.y differs for sx=+1 versus sx=-1, the local +X direction flips which way it points (forward vs. backward), so I need to account for that when placing the outer-corner lashes so they consistently point back for both eyes.

Working out the lash geometry math...

Keeping the eyeliner centered on top rather than biasing it. Now I'm adding ears as small cones near the top of the skull, tilted outward with pink inner-ear cones and tufts, then placing a forehead horn tilted forward.

Working out the horn's rotation math so it points upward and slightly forward once compounded with the head's own forward pitch, since the skull's local up-axis shifts in world space once rotated.

Still designing horn geometry...

I'll settle on combining a deep gold cone core with a pale gold helix ridge for a cleaner spiral effect, keeping the triangle count low. Now for the mane, I'm working out the neck crest geometry, computing the direction vector from the base to top of the neck and finding a perpendicular vector pointing up and back so I can offset the mane along that crest line.

For the mane tufts themselves, I'm using low-poly icosahedron shapes, cycling through pink, mint, and lavender colors, sizing them small and elongating them along the crest-perpendicular direction so they look like fluffy hair lying back and to the side, arranged in two layers for extra volume.

For the forelock, I'm placing a small ring of similarly colored tufts around the horn base at the forehead, sized smaller and positioned to curl down over the face.

Now I'm working out the tail: starting from the rump, I'm placing a short dock cylinder followed by three cascading strands of pink, mint, and lavender, each a chain of shrinking icosahedrons curving gently outward and swaying along a short 0.4m length.

I need to make sure the tail clears the hind hocks and legs, keeping it centered at x=0 while the legs sit around x≈0.11. I'll expand to 5 strands with slight x-offsets and waviness, each made of 6 tufts, giving the tail a fuller, puffier foal-like look with radius tapering slightly from top to bottom.

Now I'm working out the daisy chain necklace: it loops around the lower neck and droops in a V down the chest. I'm setting up a radial frame around the neck axis so each angle φ maps to a point at the neck's surface plus a small offset, with the front portion of the loop drooping lower than the sides to create the hanging V shape.

I'm checking whether my computed droop points actually clear the chest sphere's surface, nudging coordinates until they sit a bit outside the body for a natural loose hang rather than clipping in. I'll place the lowest front point around (0, 0.70, 0.44), slightly off the chest surface, and now work out the symmetric rear point behind the neck.

Now I'm worried the rear of the daisy chain gets swallowed by the mane tufts, since the mane's reach near the crest overlaps the chain's radius at several points along the neck. I'm considering options like widening the back of the loop, shifting the chain lower, or carving a small gap in the mane so the necklace stays visible rather than fully buried.

I'm settling on a radius function for the loop that bulges slightly at the back so the daisies sit on top of the mane, then laying out 16 daisies spaced around that curve connected by thin stem cylinders with occasional leaves, sizing most flowers around 0.07 in diameter with a slightly larger focal one at the front. Each daisy needs to face outward from the loop's center, so I'm computing an outward normal direction for orientation, adjusting for the natural droop toward the chest.

I'm designing the daisy mesh itself: a small yellow cylindrical disc for the center, surrounded by 8 flattened sphere-based petals arranged radially with a slight upward tilt for a domed look, sharing one petal geometry instance for efficiency and giving each flower a touch of random spin for variation. To keep the mesh count manageable I'm considering writing a simple geometry-merging helper so each daisy's petals combine into a single mesh rather than staying separate.

Actually, I'll skip the merge approach for now to keep things simple, accepting the mesh count tradeoff for safety.

I'm also thinking about adding a few tiny daisies woven into the mane for extra charm, scaled down from the main flower function. For the cutie mark, I'm planning a five-pointed star using extruded geometry placed on the hip, calculating the sphere surface position and rotation needed so it sits flush against the body and faces outward correctly.

For color, I'm leaning toward a gold or lilac star, possibly paired with a tiny sparkle star beside it for extra flair. I'm also sketching out a tileable canvas texture for the coat—soft radial blotches in lilac, pink, mint, and blue tones plus sparkle dots, designed to wrap seamlessly and apply nicely across the body and leg geometry via UV mapping, with repeat wrapping and proper color space settings.

Now I'm planning the full color palette for all the parts: a shared coat material using the texture, a lilac tint for lower legs to give a subtle "sock" gradient, pink for muzzle and blush areas, dark tones for nostrils and eyes with a bright highlight, gold for the horn, silver for hooves, and pastel pink/mint/lavender for mane and tail. I'm also defining colors for a daisy accent (white petals, yellow center, green stem and leaves) and the gold star, plus considering whether foal eyes should stay simple and dark without extra emissive effects.

I'm also deciding to give the coat a very subtle lilac emissive glow (low intensity) so flat shading doesn't look too dark under standard lighting, then setting low metalness and moderate roughness for the coat material. For the head, I'm laying out concrete local coordinates: a flat-shaded skull sphere, a jowl sphere for the jaw, and a tapered muzzle cylinder with specific radius and position values.

Still placing head features...

I'm reconsidering the overall head proportions and deciding to shorten the muzzle slightly so the head doesn't look disproportionately long on the foal body. Now I'm working out where the neck pivots into the skull so the pitched head angle positions correctly relative to the neck's top point.

I'm computing the actual world-space position of the nose tip after rotating the head by the pitch angle, checking it against the chest and body dimensions to make sure the head sits naturally — the height comes out around 1.5m including the horn, which seems reasonable for a stylized foal. I decide to ease the pitch down slightly to around 0.55 radians for a more natural look, then move on to defining the neck geometry connecting the base point to the new top point.

Now I'm sketching out the neck as a tapered cylinder embedded slightly into the chest and head, narrower at the top, with a helper function that builds limbs as oriented cylinders using quaternion rotation from a default up-axis to the desired direction — noting that the near-antiparallel case for legs pointing straight down is handled safely by three.js's built-in fallback.

For the legs, I'm roughing out approximate hip, knee, fetlock, and foot positions per leg with small outward/forward offsets to give the foal a splayed, wobbly stance, computing interpolation fractions along the leg for each joint based on height so the proportions read correctly as gangly newborn limbs.

For the hind legs I'm defining the hip, stifle, hock, fetlock, and coronet coordinates with their own forward/backward offsets, deriving interpolation fractions from height, and setting tapering radii for the thigh, gaskin, cannon, and pastern segments plus the hoof height.

Then for the front legs I'm sizing the forearm, knee, cannon, fetlock, pastern, and hoof segments with their own radii and shapes, using low-poly spheres for joints and a cylinder for the hoof with a silver color.

I'm adding small scaled icosahedron tufts at the fetlocks colored in alternating pastel mint, pink, and lavender for a cute "feathered" look, and leaning toward a subtle lilac shimmer that intensifies on the lower leg segments like built-in socks. For the hoof placement, I'm tilting the pastern forward slightly so the coronet sits just ahead of the fetlock, keeping the foot grounded naturally.

Now I'm shaping the torso capsule, adjusting its scale and vertical center so the body spans correctly between the legs with the withers and belly proportioned well, then adding hip and shoulder spheres to give the puppet a blocky, jointed muscle look at the haunches and shoulders. I'm deciding to skip extra belly bumps, back dips, and fuzzy body hair tufts to keep things simple.

For the mane, I'm defining positions along the neck crest using a parametric curve, placing icosahedron tufts at intervals with alternating sideways offsets, varying sizes larger near the forelock, randomized orientation, and cycling colors across three values for faceted, fluffy shading. I'm also planning small wisp cones in matching colors near the tuft ends for extra texture.

Now I'm adding hanging mane locks as elongated cones angled down and to the side, oriented via quaternion rotation so each cone's tip points away from the neck along a chosen fall direction, positioned at the midpoint between crest and tip to create a cascading lock silhouette—while being careful not to let the mane overwhelm the neck's proportions.

For the tail, I'm working out a set of five colored strands (pink, mint, lavender, mint, pink) each built from six tufts along a curved path that sways with sine functions for lateral offset and droop, with tuft radius pulsing slightly to give a fluffy look, while checking the tail's position relative to the rump and hip spheres so it reads as attached naturally to the back of the body.

Now I'm figuring out the ear geometry: small cones positioned near the top sides of the head, tilted outward and angled to counter the head's forward pitch so they read as upright, with an inner pink cone nested as a child for the ear's interior detail.

For the horn, I'm computing where its base sits on the forehead, checking it sinks slightly below the skull's surface so it looks rooted rather than floating, then working out the rotation needed so the horn's tilt combines correctly with the head's own pitch to point in the right world direction.

I'll keep the local horn rotation at zero so the overall world tilt stays around 0.55 radians (~31°), which matches a natural forward-leaning unicorn horn angle. I'm also reconsidering the proportions, leaning toward a slightly smaller, thinner horn to better suit a foal.

Now for the spiral ridge, I'm thinking through how to taper it along the horn's surface: computing helix points with about 3.5 turns, placing the ridge radius just outside the cone's radius at each height, and tapering the ridge thickness down using a sequence of small connected capsule shapes rather than a constant tube radius, so it doesn't overwhelm the horn near the tip.

I'm reconsidering a second mirrored spiral to make a classic twisted double-helix horn look, skipping floating sparkle decorations since anything hovering off the model's surface feels wrong, and instead planning subtle sparkle details directly into the coat texture plus small flat pink blush discs on the cheeks.

For the blush placement, I'm figuring out where the skull sphere's surface sits at the cheek region, computing the x-extent at that height and depth to position the discs so they sit flush against the head geometry rather than floating or sinking through it, checking that the skull curve defines the surface there rather than the jowl sphere.

Since a flat disc would leave gaps at the edges due to surface curvature, I'll switch to a small flattened ellipsoid partially embedded in the surface for a more integrated bump instead. For the eyes, I'm working out the surface position at that height and depth, sizing the eyeball sphere relatively large against the head width for a cute foal look, and flattening it along the outward axis so it protrudes naturally from the socket.

Now I'm tilting the eye rotation further forward so the eyes read as looking toward the viewer, then layering sphere-based details outward: the dark eyeball base, a purple iris slightly raised above it, a dark pupil raised further still, and small white emissive highlight spheres positioned near the top to catch light, mirrored appropriately between the two eyes.

I'm skipping eyebrows but considering eyelid and lash details using arcs and dark strokes, then checking that eyes don't collide with ears or horns before placing the eye position relative to the head pivot.

For the cutie mark, I'm realizing the hip spheres as originally sized would make the body too wide for a slender foal, so I'm shrinking their radius and pulling them inward to keep the hips proportionate, then working out where the star shape should sit on the narrower hip surface.

Now I'm calculating the exact rotation and position for the star so it sits embedded in the curved hip surface for both sides, mirroring correctly via a y-axis rotation, and accounting for the slight gap between the flat star base and the sphere's curvature by nudging the extrusion depth. I'm also confirming the mane and daisy-chain necklace are complete as a closed loop, and now I'm starting to work out the specific positions for each daisy along that loop.

Working out the neck geometry, chest capsule, and front sphere intersections so the daisy chain sits naturally against the curved surfaces...

Checking the sides and back of the chain loop against the body geometry — sides sit close to the neck radius, and the back point lands right at the top of the mane tufts, which works nicely. For spacing I'm settling on around 14-15 daisies with slight overlap so the chain reads as lush rather than sparse.

Going with N=14 daisies, alternating sizes (full and slightly smaller, radius ~0.034 and ~0.024) so the chain feels more organic, connected by thin green stem cylinders with small leaf pairs at the midpoints for texture. I'll keep most daisies white to match the classic daisy-chain look, maybe allowing just a touch of pink variation rather than a full alternating pattern.

Now I'm working out the orientation for each flower's surface normal, since a daisy facing straight out radially looks wrong on the chest versus the sides. I'm blending the radial direction with a forward-leaning bias for flowers near the front of the chest and a more sideways bias near the neck, approximating the pony's torso curvature so the flowers appear to sit naturally on the body rather than floating at odd angles.

I'm also tallying up mesh counts: each daisy with petals, center, stem, and leaf comes to roughly 154 meshes across the body garland, plus a few smaller daisies worked into the mane and forelock. Then I'm starting a rough inventory of the pony's body parts—capsule torso, chest, hips, shoulders, legs—to estimate total scene complexity.

Totaling up legs, neck, head details, eyes with lashes, horn ridges, mane tufts, tail, and all the daisies, I land around 410 meshes, which stays comfortably under my 1000-mesh budget, and triangle counts look like they'll stay well under 60k too. I'm planning to use a seeded mulberry32 RNG for consistent randomization, and now I'm writing the canvas texture function for the coat.

Writing coat texture code...

I want to keep the base texture mostly white with soft pastel blotches and sparkly star accents rather than anything too saturated, so it still reads well under flat shading across different geometry UVs, and I'm thinking about how the radial gradient blotches will look stretched along cylindrical leg UVs.

For the hair and mane I'm leaning toward a soft matte material with no extra glow, trusting standard shading to darken the pastel tones naturally in shadow. I tally up roughly twenty distinct colors across the coat, face, eyes, hooves, and decorative elements like the daisy and mane strands, then start sketching small helper functions for vector creation and mesh placement, along with a plan to share geometry instances for repeated elements like daisy petals to avoid unnecessary duplication.

For shading style, I'm deciding to use flat shading for faceted surfaces like the pearly coat and horn, but smooth shading for the eyes so they read as glossy spheres rather than faceted gems. I then sketch out a limb-building helper that takes two endpoints and radii, constructs a tapered cylinder between them, and orients it correctly using quaternion alignment, plus a blob helper for creating scaled ellipsoid shapes from a base sphere geometry.

Now I'm structuring the actual module: setting up a seeded random number generator for deterministic variation, defining the default export function that builds the root group and names it, and sketching the material palette starting with a coat material that uses a custom texture, soft emissive lilac tint, and moderate roughness to give it that pearly foal look.

Writing coat and body geometry...

Now I'm defining helper functions to compute leg joint positions, using fractional interpolation based on height to blend outward and forward offsets for hips, knees, fetlocks, and coronets, with separate logic for front and rear legs.

I'm assembling each leg segment—upper limb, knee blob, cannon, fetlock, pastern, and hoof—using tapered limb geometry and cylinder shapes for the hooves, with coat and silver coloring per segment, then starting the equivalent construction for the hind legs.

I'm defining joint positions for the hind leg (haunch, stifle, hock, fetlock, coronet) and sketching out limb segments like thigh, gaskin, hock, and calcaneus using similar tapered shapes. I'm now adjusting offset values per leg (FL, FR, HL, HR) to create a slightly asymmetric, wobbly stance by varying how far each hoof splays outward and forward or backward.

I'm setting up the neck as a tapered limb connecting shoulder base to throat top using direction vectors and radius values, then scaling it narrower on the x-axis, and checking that the neck top aligns inside the head sphere's radius without poking out — though I notice the neck is quite narrow compared to the head's width.

Now I'm placing the head's components: scaling and positioning the skull blob, jowl blob, muzzle cylinder (rotated so its axis points forward along z), nose tip blob with a pink tone for contrast against the coat color, and nostril blobs positioned symmetrically on either side, checking each piece's offsets so they nest correctly against the muzzle surface.

I'm skipping a full torus-arc mouth shape for simplicity and instead working out positions for small pink blush blobs on the cheeks, adjusting their coordinates so they sit against the jowl and skull without floating outside the head's silhouette.

Now checking the eye size and embedding depth against the skull surface curvature—deciding whether 0.046 radius feels right for a cute, big-eyed look without being too exaggerated. Next I'm planning the remaining features: ears, horn, forelock and poll tufts, and starting to sketch the horn's geometry with a tapered cone core plus a double-helix ridge pattern along its surface.

Working out the horn's ridge tube radius, turn count, and base placement so it sits partly embedded in the skull with a natural taper toward the tip. I'm considering whether to add a small collar ring at the horn's base but decide it's probably unnecessary clutter, opting instead to rely on surrounding forelock details for visual interest—then moving on to designing the forelock tufts.

I'm placing around nine colored tufts (pink, mint, lavender) in a cluster on the forehead around the horn base, checking their positions and radii against the skull surface so they sit partially embedded and drape naturally forward. I'm adding a few hanging fringe locks as small downward-angled cones between the eyes to create a cute bangs effect, then shifting focus to the mane generation logic.

Now I'm working out the mane in world coordinates rather than the head's local rotation group: computing the poll point by rotating the head-local top-back position into world space, finding the neck crest point along the spine curve, and bridging the gap between them since the mane should flow from the hidden poll tufts down onto the visible neck. I'm iterating through about twelve tuft positions along the parametrized curve, offsetting each by the surface normal scaled by curve radius plus a bit of padding, and giving them a tuft radius with slight randomness for natural variation.

For each position I'm adding a center tuft plus a side tuft offset outward and slightly lower, alternating colors between them, which gives roughly 26 tufts total. Then I'm layering in hanging locks as thin cones angled outward and downward at alternating sides, bringing the mane tuft count to about 39 plus the poll piece, each with randomized rotation and non-uniform scaling for a tousled look.

I'm also planning to scatter a few tiny daisy flowers along the mane crest at select tuft indices, tilted to follow the outward normal, and considering adding one small flower to the tail as well. Now I'm writing the daisy geometry function, building each flower from a ring of petal meshes arranged radially around a shared sphere geometry scaled per petal.

Working out petal rotation order...

Now I'm designing the daisy center and petal geometry, then setting up placement using quaternions to orient each flower along the surface normal with a random spin, and planning the stem segments connecting consecutive points in a closed chain around the neck.

For the leaves, I'm working out orientation—positioning flattened ellipsoid blobs at stem midpoints, tilted outward along a rotated tangent direction, accepting that fine roll detail won't matter much given their small size. I'm also figuring out how many daisies to place in the ring and considering that equal angular spacing won't give even arc-length spacing where the droop curvature varies.

Now I'm computing the actual droop and radius function around the loop, checking that the front of the garland hangs lower and clears the chest geometry by about 0.028 units, and verifying the side positions near the shoulders also maintain safe clearance distances from the shoulder spheres.

At the side and back positions I'm checking clearance against the neck cylinder and torso capsule, confirming the garland floats about 0.035-0.04 units clear of the neck surface and outside the torso front cap by a reasonable margin. I'm now examining whether the back portion of the loop, which sits higher near the crest, risks overlapping with the mane tufts positioned there.

Raising the back radius to 0.17 keeps the loop clearing the mane tufts and torso top, so I'm adopting a radius function that's 0.125 plus an extra 0.045 weighted toward the back of the body. I'm also confirming the hooves sit exactly at ground level and verifying the horn's tilt geometry, finding its tip projects forward to roughly z=0.75, which brings it close to the nose tip at z=0.74 — something I need to watch for overlap.

Given that overlap, I'm adjusting the horn's world tilt down to 0.45 radians so it reads more like a typical upward-forward unicorn horn rather than jutting too far toward the face, landing the tip around y=1.417, z=0.731, for a total height near 1.42m against a 0.95m withers height. Now I'm checking the ear placement on the skull, finding the ear base sits slightly outside the skull surface and needs to be pulled in closer.

Positioning ear geometry with cone shapes...

Now I'm layering the eye components—ball, iris, pupil, and highlights—checking the z-offsets so each layer peeks out past the one beneath it without being swallowed, since the pupil was getting hidden behind the iris and needed its depth pushed forward.

I'm working out which local-x direction corresponds to "front" versus "back" for each mirrored eye (sx=+1 vs sx=−1), so the highlight placement and lash direction stay consistent across both sides, then sketching the eyeliner torus geometry and its arc/rotation to sit along the top of the eye.

Now I'm defining the lashes as tapered limbs spanning from a base point on the ring to a tip offset outward and upward, with radius tapering from thick at the base to thin at the tip.

I'll add a second curling segment to each lash bending further upward for a flicked look, giving roughly 28 lash meshes total across both eyes. I'm deciding to skip eye shadow, eyebrows, and cheek fur tufts for simplicity, but keeping the star cutie mark idea with a smaller sparkle star nearby, and sanity-checking the proportions of legs, body, neck, and head size before moving on to the muzzle's downward tilt angle.

Checking the nose tip height against the withers confirms the foal's head sits in a natural lowered position typical of young ponies, and I'll leave lighting entirely to the host application rather than adding my own. For the neck, I'm computing a perpendicular vector from the spine direction to orient mane tufts correctly along the neck curve, then writing a helper function that creates icosahedron-based fur tufts with randomized scale and rotation for a shaggy look.

Writing tuft helper code...

Now I'm working through the math for tail strand placement—five colored strand groups waving with sine-based curves, tapering radius along their length, positioned to hang naturally behind the body.

I'll keep each tail strand as a single solid color rather than mixing per-tuft, cycling through mint, pink, and lavender for a layered streaked look, and apply a similar offset cycling scheme to the mane's center, side, and lock tufts. For the coat, I'm adding small cross-shaped sparkle details via canvas, and now I'm writing a helper function to build a star-shaped extrusion geometry for accessories.

I'm positioning that star on the flank with rotation aligned so it extrudes outward from the surface, layering a slightly larger lilac star beneath a smaller gold one for a sticker effect, then checking the math on hip and torso placement to make sure the star sits flush against the body surface without clipping.

Now I'm moving on to finalize the model: naming the groups for clarity, enabling cast/receive shadows across all meshes via a traversal, and starting to write out the full build function with the texture generator, seeded random utility, and root group structure that assembles the head, body, and other parts together.

Defining more materials...

Still working out leg geometry...

Now moving to the head group: I'm building the skull and muzzle shapes using blended blobs and a rotated cylinder for the muzzle, plus pink nose padding, nostrils, and cheek blush, positioning everything relative to a head group tilted forward on the neck.

Then I'm constructing the horn as its own tilted group with a tapering cone base, adding spiral ridge geometry made from a series of small tapered limb segments that wind around the horn twice, shrinking in radius toward the tip, and considering a small collar piece at the base.

For the mane, I'm planning placement of tiny daisy flower accents along the crest and near the forelock and ears, working out positions and surface normals so each daisy sits flush against the skull's curved surface without overlapping the ear or eye geometry.

Now I'm writing the daisy flower builder, generating petal and disc geometry with scaled, rotated meshes arranged radially around a center point to form a small flower shape.

Writing mane chain code...

Still writing mane tufts and locks...

Now I'm defining helper functions—blob for scaled sphere meshes, limb for cylinder bones oriented between two points, and addEye for building the layered eyeball with iris, pupil, and highlight spheres positioned and rotated to face outward and forward on each side of the head.

Writing eyeliner and eyelash code...

Still writing the ear geometry...

I'm checking that the inner ear cone pokes slightly through the outer cone for a believable layered look, and confirming the ear's outward tilt direction matches each side. Now I'm planning the canvas-based coat texture—soft pastel blotches in lilac, pink, and mint tones layered with sparkle dots to give the foal's fur a pearly, dreamlike quality, plus helper functions for placing daisies with correct orientation on the head, mane, and tail.

I'm reviewing leg joint heights and proportions to make sure the knees, hocks, fetlocks, and hooves line up correctly, then moving on to assembling the full code with materials, shadows, and all the decorative details—horn, stars, blush, daisy chain, mane, tail, and tufts—before finalizing everything into the returned root object.
